Build and run graphs

Source: R/graph.R
zl_graph.Rd

zl_graph() calls build(x) once, with x a named list of input tensors of the declared shapes, and records the tensors build() returns as the graph's outputs. Inside build(), inputs, parameters (from zl_param_tensor()) and the results of operations such as zl_crossprod() are tensors; build() is not called again, and a different input shape needs another graph.

Usage

zl_graph(build, p, inputs, loss = NULL, outputs = NULL)

zl_int(...)

zl_forward(g, data, outputs = NULL)

zl_graph_info(g)

Arguments

build

A function of one argument, the named list of inputs, returning a tensor or a named list of tensors.

p

The parameter store whose parameters build() uses.

inputs

A named list of input dimensions: numeric vectors of one to four positive whole numbers, or zl_int(...) for an integer input.

loss

The name of a scalar output to train on (see the training functions); NULL for none.

outputs

The names of the outputs to keep, of those build() returns; NULL for all.

...

Dimensions, for zl_int().

g

A graph.

data

A named list of arrays, one per input, each matching its input's dimensions exactly (a plain vector for a one-dimensional input). NA is refused.

Value

zl_graph() returns a graph of class zl_graph; zl_int() an input specification; zl_forward() a named list of double arrays; zl_graph_info() a list describing the graph.

Details

zl_forward() writes data into the inputs, runs the graph and returns the outputs as double arrays. The inputs are rewritten in place on every call, so a graph runs any number of times without being rebuilt.

Inputs are single-precision (f32) unless declared with zl_int(), which makes them 32-bit integers (i32) for zl_get_rows() and zl_rope(). Integer indices count from 0, as in 'ggml'.

Examples

p <- zl_params()
zl_param(p, "w", c(3, 2))
g <- zl_graph(
  function(x) zl_relu(zl_crossprod(zl_param_tensor(p, "w"), x$input)),
  p,
  inputs = list(input = c(3, 5))
)
out <- zl_forward(g, list(input = matrix(1, 3, 5)))
dim(out$output)
#> [1] 2 5
